title: Britain after 1947
hook: Sikhs settle in Southall, Birmingham and the mill towns, building gurdwaras in old houses

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhagat Singh Thind: a veteran told he couldn't be a citizen, who stayed, taught, and became one. Your line was he belonged. Today we cross the Atlantic, to a gray, rainy Britain after the war. Day three hundred eighteen.

Picture a row of narrow brick houses in an English town in the 1960s. Every house the same: a front door, a bay window, a little back yard. But one of them is different on a Sunday morning. Shoes are piled up by the front step. Men with covered heads and women in bright scarves are going in and out. From an upstairs window, if you listen, you can hear singing and a tabla. And there's a smell of cooking that doesn't belong to any English Sunday lunch. Today: Britain after 1947.
screen: `A ROW OF BRICK HOUSES.` → `SHOES PILED BY ONE FRONT STEP.` → `SINGING FROM AN UPSTAIRS WINDOW.`

segments.voice: After the Second World War, Britain was short of workers. Factories, foundries and mills needed hands. And after Partition, many Punjabi families had lost land and needed a new start. So from the 1950s, Sikh men came to Britain, often one from a village first, then his brothers and cousins. They worked in the foundries of Birmingham and the West Midlands, in the textile mills of Yorkshire and Lancashire, in the factories and at the airport near Southall in west London. They shared crowded houses to save money. In the 1960s, wives and children joined them. Later, more Sikh families came from Kenya and Uganda. Now the gurdwaras. There had been a gurdwara in London since before the First World War, but for most of these new towns there was nothing. So Sikhs did what they had done in Hong Kong and California: they bought an ordinary house. Upstairs, the front bedroom became the room of the Guru Granth Sahib. Downstairs, the front room was for the sangat to sit, and the kitchen made langar. Every morning someone performed the parkash, opening the Guru for the day, and every evening laid it to rest. A house became a gurdwara. Later, as the community grew, they bought old churches, cinemas and factories, and eventually built large gurdwaras of their own. But many British Sikhs still remember that first house, and the older ones will tell you: it wasn't the building. Wherever the Guru is honored and the sangat gathers, that's a gurdwara.
screen: `BRITAIN NEEDS WORKERS.` · `FOUNDRIES, MILLS, SOUTHALL.` · `AN ORDINARY HOUSE, BOUGHT.` · `THE GURU UPSTAIRS, LANGAR BELOW.` · then, large: `A HOUSE BECAME A GURDWARA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a building with new eyes. Settle, and breathe. Picture a building you pass often without thinking: an old shop, a house, a hall on your street. Now wonder about it. Who might have gathered there? What might have been sung, cooked, prayed, celebrated inside? Let ordinary walls become full of people and stories. Then think of your own home. What makes it sacred to someone? Rest with that. The bell holds the time.
Britain after 1947. Sikhs came to work in the foundries, mills and factories, and turned ordinary houses into gurdwaras.
Your line: a house became a gurdwara. Today, look at one ordinary building you pass and wonder who gathers there. Day three hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: In Britain, many gurdwaras began in terraced houses, and later in converted churches, cinemas and factories; each morning the Guru Granth Sahib is opened (parkash) and each night it is laid to rest.

fork.setup: it's the 1960s. your Sikh community in an English mill town has grown, but there's no gurdwara. what do you do?

wait until you can afford a new building.
fork.reveal: many communities bought a terraced house: the Guru upstairs, the sangat in the front room, langar in the kitchen.

original.note: Gurmukhi: parkash, light; the morning ceremony of opening the Guru Granth Sahib.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gurdwara is a special building.
what it means: wherever the Guru is honored and the sangat gathers, even a terraced house.
what a scholar hears: London had a gurdwara from 1911; the large-scale settlement of the 1950s–60s followed postwar labor shortages and chain migration from Punjabi villages.

sources.ref: Sikh Rehat Maryada on parkash and sukhasan of the Guru Granth Sahib

notes: The first gurdwara in London (Putney, 1911, moving to Shepherd's Bush in 1913) is compressed to 'since before the First World War'; confirm.
Employment patterns (West Midlands foundries, Yorkshire and Lancashire mills, Southall factories and Heathrow) are the usual summary; confirm.
'Gray' is used in the review as American spelling.
